rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods <U+2013> authors grew sweet corn in 25 L soil columns in fall 2004 and spring 2006 with three fertilizer-N residence-time treatments (1, 3, 7 d before a forced weekly leaching event) and measured weekly N uptake, biomass, root length density, ear yield and FUE (Table 1, Fig. 4-6).
rows.notes: Primary column experiment, but no soil sensor or irrigation-scheduling treatment was tested; irrigation was applied uniformly by drip and leaching was imposed artificially with ~2 pore volumes of water. The treatment variable is N residence time, which the authors only describe as 'indicative of better irrigation practices'. The study shows that longer N residence time increased growth, yield, N uptake and FUE (e.g., total dry matter 26 vs 81 g/plant in fall, 28 vs 108 g/plant in spring for tR-1 vs tR-7); it reports nothing on crop water stress (columns were kept near field capacity) nor on sensor-based or high-frequency irrigation scheduling. Technology in the passage (soil sensor / irrigation scheduling) is not the one studied.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods <U+2013> own column experiment (two seasons, four replicates, three residence-time treatments) with measured leachate N and plant N; potential N leaching calculated as applied N minus plant uptake (Fig. 7).
rows.notes: Primary study, but no soil sensor and no irrigation-scheduling treatment; leaching was deliberately imposed by flushing columns with 2 pore volumes of water at 1, 3 or 7 d after fertigation. The study shows that longer N residence time reduced calculated potential cumulative N leaching (253/223/101 kg N/ha in fall and 282/159/85 kg N/ha in spring for tR-1/3/7), and the authors infer that better irrigation management would extend residence time, but this is an inference rather than a tested effect of sensor-based or frequent small-volume irrigation on leaching in sandy soil. Leaching values are calculated differences, not measured under an irrigation-scheduling treatment.

notes: Full text available and complete. The study is a controlled column experiment on fertilizer-N residence time in sweet corn on Candler fine sand; it does not involve soil moisture sensors or any comparison of irrigation scheduling regimes, so both claim rows are technology mismatches.
